passage_text: Researchers studied the effect of a novel cognitive enhancer on reaction time in healthy adults. A double‑blind, placebo‑controlled trial enrolled 120 participants who were randomly assigned to one of four groups: placebo (control), low dose (10 mg), medium dose (20 mg), or high dose (40 mg). Each participant completed a computerized simple reaction time task 30 minutes after drug administration. The mean reaction times (RT) and standard deviations (SD) for each group are presented in Table 1. The study aimed to determine whether increasing doses would produce a dose‑response improvement in RT without compromising safety. All participants reported no adverse events, and the study was approved by the institutional review board.
table_data:
Table 1. Mean Reaction Time (ms) by Dose

Condition | Mean RT | SD
Control (Placebo) | 350 | 15
Low Dose (10 mg) | 340 | 12
Medium Dose (20 mg) | 330 | 10
High Dose (40 mg) | 320 | 8
stem: Based on Table 1, which statement best describes the observed dose‑response relationship?

options.A: Reaction time increases as dose increases.
options.B: Reaction time decreases as dose increases.
options.C: Reaction time is unchanged across all doses.
options.D: Reaction time is lowest in the low‑dose group.

explanation: The mean RT decreases from 350 ms (control) to 320 ms (high dose), indicating faster responses with higher doses.
trap: Students may mistakenly focus on the SD values and ignore the mean differences.

stem: Which feature described in the passage best ensures that the observed changes in reaction time are attributable to the drug dose?

options.A: Random assignment of participants to dose groups
options.B: Using a larger sample size than 120 participants
options.C: Measuring reaction time at multiple time points
options.D: Including a crossover design where participants receive all doses

explanation: Correct: Random assignment to the dose groups balances participant characteristics, so reaction-time differences can be attributed to dose. Why the others are wrong: B) a larger sample improves precision but does not balance the groups. C) measuring at multiple time points is not described (reaction time was measured once, 30 minutes after dosing). D) a crossover design is not described; separate groups received separate doses.
trap: Overvaluing the crossover design, which the passage does not describe; separate groups were randomly assigned, and that random assignment is what balances confounders.

trap: Dividing the 30 ms drop by the high-dose mean (320) or confusing it with the 10 ms step between adjacent doses (2.9%), instead of dividing by the control mean of 350.

stem: Which of the following statements is a common misinterpretation of the standard deviation values in Table 1?

options.A: The SD indicates the variability of reaction times within each dose group.
options.B: A smaller SD in the high‑dose group suggests less variability in responses.
options.C: The SD values can be used to calculate confidence intervals for the mean.
options.D: The SD values show that the high‑dose group had the fastest reaction times.

explanation: SD reflects variability, not speed; option D incorrectly equates SD with mean performance.
trap: Students may confuse SD with mean RT, thinking lower SD means faster responses.

stem: Which test is most appropriate for comparing mean reaction time between the placebo group and the high-dose group in this design?
explanation: Correct: A) The groups are separate participants and the outcome (RT in ms) is continuous, so an independent-samples t-test compares the two means. Why the others are wrong: B) A paired t-test needs the same participants measured twice. C) Chi-square tests compare categorical counts. D) McNemar tests paired binary outcomes.
trap: Choosing the paired t-test because two means are being compared; the participants in the two groups are different people, so the samples are independent.
